article.title: Age at First Measles-Mumps-Rubella Vaccination in Children With Autism and School-Matched Control Subjects: A Population-Based Study in Metropolitan Atlanta

candidates.rawAssertion: Most case (70.5%) and control children (67.5%) were vaccinated between 12 and 17 months of age.
More case (93.4%) than control children (90.6%) were vaccinated before 36 months.
The association between vaccination before 36 months and autism was strongest in the 3- to 5-year age group.
The Institute of Medicine reviewed the MMR-autism hypothesis and rejected a causal association at the population level.
In 1996, the Metropolitan Atlanta Developmental Disabilities Surveillance Program identified 987 children 3 to 10 years of age with autism, for a prevalence of 3.4 per 1000 children.
The study included 624 case children and 1824 control children.
The study was approved by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s institutional review board.

The MADDSP data files were reviewed by a developmental pediatrician to identify subgroups of children with potentially different susceptibilities to development of autism from an environmental exposure.
Children without any indication of developmental delay before 12 months of age were grouped into a single category.
The overall distributions of ages at first MMR vaccination were similar (P = .22) for case and control children.
Vaccination before 18 months or 24 months of age was not associated with case status, either overall or in the different gender or age subgroups.
The odds ratio for case children vaccinated before 36 months was 1.49 (95% CI: 1.04 –2.14).
The proportion of case children with regression was lower than reported in other studies.
The routinely recommended infant vaccines that used to contain thimerosal were diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis, hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b.
MMR vaccine has never contained thimerosal.
The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act mandated the provision of special education programs for children with autism beginning at approximately 36 months of age.
The study found that the age at time of first MMR administration was similar among case and control children.
A majority of case children who were vaccinated after 36 months of age had indications of developmental problems before 36 months of age.
